blocks.text: Cybersecurity awareness means understanding how to protect computers, networks and data from attacks. As people rely more on technology, cyber threats have become common; hackers use tricks and harmful software to steal information or damage systems. Knowing how to detect, prevent and respond to threats keeps personal and organisational data secure: for example, install antivirus software, and avoid public Wi-Fi for online banking or other sensitive work.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Avoid offensive language, spam and sharing confidential information.

Cyber threats are actions or programs that target computers and networks to steal information, damage systems or interrupt services. Knowing how they work helps users spot early warning signs; most attacks can be avoided by safe browsing, antivirus software and care with emails and links. Recognising threats is the first step in protection.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Phishing is among the most common attacks.

blocks.caption: Common types of cyberattack
rows: Spreads through infected files and can damage or delete data
Fake emails, messages or websites trick people into giving passwords or personal details
Locks files or systems and demands payment to unlock them
Floods a website with traffic from many computers until it crashes

blocks.text: Cyberattacks harm both individuals, who may lose files, passwords or money, and organisations, which may suffer data breaches, stopped operations, lost customer trust, damaged reputation and financial loss. Schools and hospitals can be affected too.

blocks.alt: Five coloured boxes describe common attacks: virus (spreads through infected files; damages or deletes data), phishing (fake emails or sites trick you into giving passwords), ransomware (locks your files and demands payment), spyware (secretly collects your information) and DDoS attack (floods a website with traffic until it crashes). A side box lists the harm to people and to organisations.
blocks.caption: Common cyberattacks and their harm (original diagram after 9.2).
blocks.long_description: Phishing attacks people rather than machines, which is why awareness matters as much as software.

items: Two-factor authentication (2FA): two forms of verification before access, for example a password and then a code sent to the phone or email. A stolen password alone is no longer enough.
Biometric verification: physical features such as fingerprints, face scans or voice patterns confirm identity.
Firewall: a barrier between a computer and the Internet that lets safe data through and blocks harmful traffic.
Intrusion detection system (IDS): monitors a network for suspicious activity and alerts users to possible threats.
Antivirus software: scans files and removes viruses and other malware before they cause damage.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Simulate logging in to an account with a second step (a code from the teacher) to understand how 2FA works.

blocks.alt: Four nested rings around 'your data': firewall (outer), IDS, antivirus and login (inner), with a key: firewall blocks harmful traffic; IDS spots suspicious activity; antivirus removes malware; login uses 2FA and biometrics. A side box shows two-factor authentication: 1 password (something you know) then 2 code sent to your phone, with a phone showing a six-digit code; biometrics such as fingerprint, face or voice are something you are. A stolen password alone is not enough to get in.
blocks.caption: Layers of protection and two-factor authentication (original diagram after 9.2).
blocks.long_description: Each layer stops what the others miss, an idea called defence in depth.

blocks.text: Data protection means keeping digital information safe from unauthorised access, loss or damage, so that only the right people can see or use it. Cryptography is the science of securing information so only authorised users can understand it. Encryption turns readable data into coded text using a key; decryption turns it back when needed. An intercepted encrypted message is unreadable, so cryptography is used in secure websites, online banking and messaging apps.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Secure storage and transmission prevent unauthorised access and data breaches.

blocks.alt: HELLO (readable plaintext) passes through encrypt (with a key) to become KHOOR (coded ciphertext), then through decrypt (with the key) to become HELLO again. A dashed arrow from KHOOR shows that an attacker who intercepts the message sees only KHOOR. A note: a toy example shifting each letter 3 places (key = 3); real systems use long secret keys and strong mathematics, as in HTTPS, online banking and messaging apps.
blocks.caption: Encryption and decryption with a key (original diagram after 9.2).
blocks.long_description: The shift-by-3 code is called a Caesar cipher; it is easy to break by trying all 25 shifts, which is why real encryption uses much stronger methods.

blocks.text: Data must be protected both when stored and when sent. Encrypted connections such as HTTPS protect data in transit, cloud storage services encrypt saved files, and regular backups protect against loss from system failure or attack.

An intrusion is unauthorised access to a computer or network, often through a weakness. Vulnerabilities are weaknesses in software, hardware or user behaviour; warning signs include unexpected slowdowns, unknown programs and strange network traffic. Checking system logs and using scanning tools find these signs early. When a problem is found, troubleshooting finds its cause, and preventive measures follow: firewalls, antivirus and anti-malware, updating software, changing passwords, removing harmful files and, if needed, restoring data from backups. Documenting the problem and the fix helps stop it happening again.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Look at sample system logs or screenshots and find suspicious actions.

blocks.prompt: You receive an email saying 'Your bank account is locked. Click here and enter your PIN within 1 hour.' What type of attack is this, and what should you do?
blocks.explanation: Phishing: it creates urgency and asks for secret details through a link. Do not click or reply; contact the bank through its official number or app, report the email, and delete it. Banks never ask for a PIN by email.

items: Threats: virus, phishing, ransomware, spyware, DDoS; they harm people and organisations.
Cryptography: encryption and decryption with a key; HTTPS and encrypted storage; watch for vulnerabilities, troubleshoot and prevent.
